extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of public opinion, political scientists, journalists, and readers interested in media and political psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Examine how individuals' simplified mental 'pictures' (the pseudo-environment) are formed, how they mislead or guide political behavior, and what limits their accuracy. Emphasizes causes (limited facts, stereotypes, symbolic personalities) and consequences for democratic decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic_personalities_as_centers_of_public_feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Worldwide concentration on a symbolic personality (heroes or villains) organizes and intensely focuses the emotions of whole populations; e.g., Joffre as 'Savior of the World' or the Kaiser/Lenin/Trotsky as incarnations of evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs especially in intense phases of war when fear and hatred dominate; such symbols 'incarnate' victory or evil and can organize the emotion of large groups. In more normal times symbols are more fragmented and subject to comparison and argument. Examples: wartime hero-worship, crafted photographic props for generals, letters from naive admirers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-environment_vs_real_environment
rubrics_metrics.description: People act on a 'pseudo-environment'—the representation of the world in their minds—rather than the full, complex real environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pseudo-environment is constructed from limited, selected information and imagination; it governs thought and emotion until action forces confrontation with reality. Social analysts should study how the pseudo-environment is put together rather than assume the real environment is readily known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictions_are_representations_not_necessarily_lies
rubrics_metrics.description: 'By fictions I do not mean lies.' Fictions range 'all the way from complete hallucination to the scientists' perfectly self-conscious use of a schematic model.' They are representations of the environment used to guide action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the constructive role of fictions: they enable reasoning under complexity by simplifying; they may be useful (scientific models) or misleading (hallucinations), and are not identical with deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action_exposes_maladjustment_when_pseudo-facts_meet_reality
rubrics_metrics.description: When stimuli from the pseudo-environment lead to practical actions, contradiction with the real environment generates rapid correction or 'maladjustment'—the 'murder of a Beautiful Theory by a Gang of Brutal Facts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoughts and emotions may persist long without change, but actions produce immediate tests; policy and social action reveal inaccuracies of the pictures and compel learning by experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited_facts_and_information_availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy of public pictures is limited by the facts available to individuals—their access to events, scale, and relevant data is often inadequate (e.g., no one can imagine three million men on a front; ordinary citizens latch onto individuals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because most people lack professional access (maps, orders of battle), they simplify complex events into manageable images; journalists and communicators should note how scarcity of facts shapes public perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time_attention_and_compression_constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The short time available to many people to attend to public affairs forces compression of information into brief messages and simplified images, limiting fidelity to complex reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public communication is often compressed into headlines, short dispatches, or slogans; such compression fosters simplification and hampers accurate understanding of complicated events or relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stored_images_stereotypes_and_prejudices_as_interpreters
rubrics_metrics.description: Incoming facts are interpreted through 'stored images, stereotypes, and prejudices' which fill out and powerfully direct attention and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receivers do not encounter neutral data; they have preformed interpretive frameworks that shape what they notice and how they infer causes. This explains why rumors and unverified tales spread and are accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic_construction_of_good_and_evil (exorcism_of_devils)
rubrics_metrics.description: The same mechanism that creates heroes also constructs figures who are seen as sources of all evil; social minds attribute diverse misfortunes or events to these personal symbols (exorcism of devils).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simplifies causal explanation (strikes, obstructions, fires all wind back to a personal source), fueling hostility and policy responses based on symbolic attribution rather than complex causal analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity_of_private_worlds_undermines_stable_unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals and groups inhabit varied private 'worlds'—different knowledge, beliefs, and schemes of interpretation—so expecting uniform thought while expecting uniform action is 'a doubtful speculation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social unity depends on coincidence of action more than shared inner picture; policy-makers must understand that heterogeneous beliefs may still produce coordinated action under certain conditions, but instability remains likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid_nature_of_pseudo-environment (nature_and_conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pseudo-environment is a hybrid 'compounded of "human nature" and "conditions"'; one cannot explain behavior solely by innate traits or external conditions without considering how the world is represented to actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simplistic nature-vs-nurture conclusions; the forms of the pseudo-environment mediate how people respond to opportunities and stimuli, so analysts must study both psychological predispositions and the informational/representational context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role_of_propaganda_and_formation_of_group-consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda operates by creating and substituting new pictures to which people respond (e.g., Marxian hope placed on propaganda to form class-consciousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand propaganda as image-shaping: it aims to replace one set of representations with another to alter motives and behaviors. Analysts and communicators should examine how deliberate messaging constructs shared images and identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyst_vs_psychoanalyst_criteria_for_normality
rubrics_metrics.description: The social analyst should not adopt the psychoanalyst's implicit criterion of a 'normal biological career' based on an assumed knowable environment; instead, the sociologist must study how public opinion itself conceives the environment and forms its criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating public opinions, do not judge them by an assumed 'normal' standard detached from the existing social representations; study the formation and function of the pseudo-environment as the proper object of analysis.
